newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Political woes loom for Albania as troops arriving.
newsitem.headline: Political woes loom for Albania as troops arriving.

text.p: Self-styled "salvation committees" controlling much of southern Albania are muddying the waters for political parties trying to prepare for a general election they hope to hold at the end of June.
More troops, meanwhile, were arriving in the chaotic Balkan nation in the build-up of an Italian-led, United Nations-sanctioned multinational force mandated to secure aid shipments.
A contingent of more than 700 Greek soldiers were expected to land in the port of Durres near Tirana on Friday and to travel on by land to the port of Vlore in the rebel-held south.
The 6,000-strong force, which also includes troops from Turkey, Spain, Romania, Denmark and Austria, is expected to become fully operational within three weeks.
International mediator Franz Vranitzky, a former Austrian chancellor, said on Thursday that the problem of dealing with the salvation committees was dividing the nation's political parties.
"That is certainly the hardest part about the whole election process," Vranitzky, an envoy of the Organisation for the Security and Cooperation in Europe, told reporters.

He said President Sali Berisha and all political parties had agreed that they wanted to hold the vote on June 29, but stressed there were still many differences that had to be overcome before the election could go ahead.
Parties had to come up with a common strategy on the rebel committees as well as the procedure to be used in the vote.
Rebels, demanding Berisha's resignation, seized control of much of the south in a widespread insurrection following the collapse of dubious savings schemes earlier this year.

Banditry is rife. A small group of Italian troops sent to Vlore on Thursday to secure the port were welcomed by a local gang leader, described by locals as a drug-trafficker, who said: "You are my brothers. If you need help, you can ask me."
Gunfire and explosions were heard around the southern town throughout the day but the troops were never in any serious danger, witnesses said.
The Greek troops are expected in Vlore at the weekend and will be the first sizeable contingent to arrive in southern Albania since the U.N.-backed Operation Alba mission was launched on Tuesday.

It has a mandate to protect deliveries of humanitarian aid, destined first for orphanages and old peoples homes. The U.N.'s food aid agency, the World Food Programme, hopes to begin delivery of 400 tonnes of flour and beans by the weekend.
Another 600 French troops and 200 vehicles were also expected to arrive in Durres on Friday. The French will then be at their full complement of some 1,000 men.
Italian spokesman Lieutenant Colonel Gianfranco Scalas said the mission was moving at "full speed". He said: "We are very content with the start of the mission."
Vranitzky, who held two days of talks with Berisha and political figures to try to overcome differences hampering the progress towards elections, said he was also satisfied.
"I think that we have achieved some progress today."
However in Vienna, Foreign Minister Niels Helveg Petersen of Denmark, the OSCE chairman-in-office, said much work still remained to ensure the poll was of a high quality.
"Clearly, we all realise that elections are extremely important to provide Albania with a new democratic structure and we should move ahead as fast as at all possible," he said.
"How fast it can be done is as yet not clear."
